in_text_mentions: A 47-year-old Caucasian female presented with a 5-year-history bluish-grey pigmentation of the right conjunctiva, sclera, and eyelids (Figure 1). As observed from her previous annual ophthalmic examination, the intraocular pressure never exceeded 16 mmHg, and the optic nerve head appeared normal in both eyes. Gonioscopy showed wide open and medium pigmented chamber angle with all elements of angle visible. Humphrey visual fields and optical coherence tomography findings did not show glaucoma damage. Her medical history included high blood pressure.

The article title and in-text confirm the patient has nevus of Ota (oculodermal melanocytosis), and the ocular-surface pigmentation is its ocular melanocytosis manifestation. The closest vocabulary finding is scleral/episcleral melanocytosis; the precise caption term 'conjunctival melanosis' is proposed as it is absent from the vocabulary. B: Anterior-segment ophthalmic photograph of the right eye showing conjunctival melanosis of the inferior bulbar conjunctiva. in_text_mentions: The patient underwent a comprehensive ocular examination. Visual acuity was reduced, measuring 20/100 in the right eye (OD) and 20/30 in the left eye (OS). Anterior segment evaluation (Figure 1) revealed conjunctival melanosis in the right eye (graded as melanosis++), a clear cornea and anterior chamber, and the presence of a posterior chamber intraocular lens (PCIOL) in the right eye, indicating prior cataract extraction. Pupils were round and reactive to light, and there was no relative afferent pupillary defect (RAPD). Intraocular pressure was within normal limits (13 mmHg OD, 11 mmHg OS).
